CITY OF READING, OHIO
COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES – REGULAR SESSION
SEPTEMBER 01, 2026 – 7:30 PM 
Page 1 09-01-2026 Reading Council Minutes 
For the full detail of this evening’s Council Meeting, please visit www.watchreadingohio.com . 
CALL TO ORDER 
President of Council, Kevin Mattscheck, called the meeting to order at 7:30 PM. 
INVOCATION AND PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE 
President of Council, Kevin Mattscheck, led those in attendance in a prayer and then the Pledge of Allegiance. 
ROLL CALL 
Council Members Present: Mr. Powell, Mr. Bronner, Mr. Bishop, Mr. Boehner, Mr. Thamann, Mrs. Kroeger, 
& Mrs. Eadicicco. 
OTHER CITY OFFICIALS PRESENT: 
Mayor Bo Bemmes, Law Director Dave Stevenson, Treasurer Brenda Owens, Auditor Sabrina Smith 
& Clerk of Council Carla Bronner. 
President of Council, Kevin Mattscheck announced that the previously scheduled Public Hearing regarding the 
Zoning Code Ordinance, had been cancelled for the evening. It was announced the ordinance will be reviewed 
again, and that potential additional items will be added. A revised ordinance will be forthcoming, as will the 
announcement of a scheduled Public Hearing. 
Motion made by Dave Powell, seconded by Mr. Bronner, to “table” the scheduled third reading of the Zoning 
Code Ordinance. Motion carried by a 7-0 roll call vote. 
APPROVAL OF MINUTES: Motion to approve the August 18, 2026, Council Meeting Minutes made by Mrs. 
Eadicicco, seconded by Mr. Boehner. Motion carried by voice vote. 
AUDIENCE ASKING PARTICIPATION: 
(1) Bob Ashbrock - stated that although the public hearing had been canceled, he had prepared written remarks 
that he believes are important for Council to consider. He planned to submit the comments to the clerk and 
requested that they be distributed to Council members and included in the meeting minutes. 
(2) Reece Halden - raised concerns about Reading’s use of Flock automated license plate readers, particularly 
regarding third-party access to and sharing of data. He cited concerns in other Ohio communities, including 
Dayton, where police officials reportedly discovered inadequate oversight of third-party access and subsequently 
canceled their Flock contract and removed the cameras. 
Halden urged Reading City Council to establish greater oversight and transparency regarding the cameras, 
including determining who has access to the data, how widely information is shared, and what safeguards are in 
place to prevent misuse. He emphasized that residents should have access to this information and assurance that 
the technology is being properly monitored. 
(3) Maggie: Strongly opposes Reading’s use of Flock automated license plate reader cameras, citing concerns

about privacy, surveillance, potential misuse, inaccurate AI systems, and constitutional rights. She brought up 
that other communities have begun canceling Flock contracts because of similar concerns and she also expressed 
broader concerns about mass surveillance and the potential for government or private entities to monitor 
individuals’ behavior and political or personal beliefs. She referenced Ohio House Bill 249 and federal policies 
concerning domestic terrorism as examples of changing definitions of acceptable conduct and expression, arguing 
that surveillance technology could become more concerning if laws change. 
Maggie questioned whether City Council adequately considered the consequences of purchasing Flock cameras in 
2024. She noted that Council members had previously requested measurable results to justify the approximately 
$15,000 annual cost and information showing how frequently Flock data was used in investigations. 
According to her, this information has not been adequately provided through the city’s transparency portal, and 
many camera records do not include case numbers. She also questioned whether the cameras have produced any 
measurable reduction in crime since their installation. 
Maggie criticized the process by which Council approved the Flock cameras, noting that all seven Council 
members voted in favor of the purchase on March 19, 2024, after a third reading was bypassed and an emergency 
was declared. They argued that this provided limited opportunity for public input before the cameras were 
approved. She also contended that concerns raised by Council members and residents were not adequately 
addressed before the vote and called for greater transparency regarding how the technology is being used. 
Maggie concluded by arguing that private surveillance contracts should not replace constitutional protections or 
warrants. She urged Council to prioritize residents’ privacy and civil liberties, reconsider the use of Flock 
technology in light of what has been learned since 2024, terminate the Flock contract, and remove the cameras. 
Mark Bishop Response: The discussion surrounding Flock cameras is becoming unavoidable nationwide, and 
there is a need to determine where appropriate limits should be established. As larger cities, the federal 
government, courts, and state governments continue addressing the issue, there should be greater clarity regarding 
how the law will be interpreted in relation to these types of cameras. This information will help the Council make 
responsible decisions that allow citizens of Reading to feel safe while also protecting the liberty and privacy they 
deserve. 
Katie Eadicicco Response: Made a motion to refer the issue of Flock cameras to her committee for review. Mr. 
Bishop seconded the motion. Mr. Boehner brought up the position that he believes this topic belongs in the 
Public Health & Safety committee for review. Motion carried by a 6-1 voice vote (Mr. Boehner voting “no”). 
Motion made by Mr. Powell, seconded by Mrs. Kroeger, to ALSO put the topic and review of FLOCK Cameras 
into the Public Health & Safety committee. Motion carried by 7-0 voice vote. 
(4) Sue Renderly - expressed concerns about privacy and potential misuse of Flock cameras, citing recent reports 
of excessive license-plate searches and calls by some officials to remove the technology. 
(5) Mary – questioned whether Flock cameras are appropriate or necessary for a smaller community like

Reading, noting that they are more commonly associated with larger cities. They requested that City Council 
review 20 years of local crime statistics, specifically for murder, rape, kidnapping, and physical assault, and use 
that information to help evaluate whether Flock cameras are justified in Reading.

There will be a public hearing during our City Council meeting on Tuesday October 20th at 7:30pm to review a

The contract agreement between Reading and Sycamore Township will be available by the end of this week for

Mark Bishop and I attended a Hamilton County Municipal League meeting on August 22 to listen to our Ohio 
Municipal League president Kent Scarrett speak about the incredible importance of protecting our Home 
Rule authority that allows local governments to make our own decisions in the best interest of our residents. Kent 
mentioned the future of property taxes, data centers, shared services, State Governments idea of 
having fewer local governments and schools, school funding and unfunded State mandates. The Ohio Municipal 
League is a very valuable asset for us as they monitor all the issues being considered at the State 
level and analyze them for us. 
Please call me anytime with any City related questions, comments or concerns at 513-509-8619.

ZONING, PLANNING & ENVIRONMENT: Dave Powell: 
- My committee met prior to the previous Council meeting. The primary discussion involved the possibility of 
establishing regulations for food trucks. Assistant Fire Chief O’Connor developed an initial outline, and the 
committee is reviewing the proposed regulations and determining how to proceed. 
The committee also discussed the zoning ordinance that was tabled this evening due to procedural issues related 
to its approval. The ordinance will return to the Planning Commission for revisions and further consideration. 
As part of that review, the committee is considering incorporating food truck regulations into the zoning 
ordinance. An additional issue raised by Randy Cook will also be addressed during the revision process. 
Once the Planning Commission holds its public hearing, the matter will return to Council for review. The 
committee anticipates that the revised ordinance and related issues will come back before Council later this fall.

RECREATION: Scott Thamann: 
We have concluded our community pool season. For our income: memberships, concessions, guest fees and swim 
lessons brought in roughly $53,334. Our expenses for concessions and cleaning supplies, pool chemicals, and 
salaries cost us roughly $102,700, which results in a deficit of $48,300. This deficit is normal, and it shows the 
city’s commitment to providing affordable recreation opportunities in our community. 
We have received several bids for a new track, and a decision should be coming soon.
